newsitem.title: USA: Simpson civil trial unfolded under TV blackout.
newsitem.headline: Simpson civil trial unfolded under TV blackout.

text.p: O.J. Simpson's criminal trial was televised gavel to gavel. His civil trial unfolded under a TV blackout, but many Americans still followed every twist and turn.

The former football star's second trial culminated late on Tuesday with a verdict that nearly collided with President Bill Clinton's State of the Union address. "Television's worst nightmare," wrote Los Angeles Times television columnist Howard Rosenberg.

Unable to show viewers what was happening inside the courtroom and already committed to broadcasting Clinton's speech live, the major networks ended up relaying the first word of the jury's decision in lines of text sent crawling across TV screens as the president spoke.

It was a far cry from Oct. 3, 1995, when much of America watched on live television as Simpson was acquitted in the murders of his ex-wife, Nicole Brown Simpson, and her friend, Ronald Goldman. The sensational trial had rivaled the aftermath of the Kennedy assassination and the first moon landing as America's most-watched television events.

Cameras were banned from Simpson's ensuing civil trial, depriving millions of viewers of the chance to witness the reading of the verdicts that declared the former football star "liable" for the deaths. But despite that, public interest in the case remained high.

Consider the way cable station E! Entertainment TV recreated each day's testimony using actors reading actual court transcripts. "When the judge made the ruling 'No cameras' we knew one thing: our viewers wanted to be back inside the courtroom," said John Rieber, vice president of programming for E! "They had a chance to follow it every day (in 1995) and that was taken away from them."
He added, "We have had phenomenal feedback, our ratings have been double or triple the normal average for the time period."

Neither has the lack of cameras and a gag order on lawyers and witnesses lessened the "made-for-TV" histrionics, veteran journalist Steve Dunleavy said. "Critics said the criminal trial had Hollywood hysteria but these lawyers are hardly holding back -- (plaintiffs' attorney Daniel) Petrocelli sounded like something out of Hamlet," he said.

"I don't think TV cameras committed the crimes some people thought. The high-octane level on both sides has not been dimmed by the fact that there are no cameras," said Dunleavy, a New York Post columnist who also does commentaries for tabloid TV shows.

Judge Hiroshi Fujisaki made it clear from the start that he would not tolerate the circus atmosphere that surrounded the criminal case under Judge Lance Ito, with attorneys holding press conferences to put their spin on proceedings.

He barred lawyers, witnesses and parties to the lawsuit from discussing it in public and banned TV and photographers from the courtroom, saying the TV camera in the criminal trial had "significantly diverted and distracted the participants."

Laurie Levenson, Loyola University law professor, disagrees that the camera was to blame for the antics of the first trial. "It is not so much the TV cameras or lack of them. Judge Fujisaki has made the difference," she said.
"The public would have had a different perspective of the justice system if they had seen this trial (on TV). They would have seen the different evidence. The judge conducted this one differently."

CNN's Greta van Susteren, whose daily show on legal issues called "A Burden of Proof" grew out of coverage of the Simpson criminal trial, said she was concerned about the perception viewers had this time. "The difference? The public didn't get to see this one," she said.
There is no denying the theatrical nature of the criminal trial made stars of some of the participants. TV made many of them household names and several wrote books.

The two legal protagonists -- prosecutor Marcia Clark and defence attorney Johnnie Cochran -- even landed their own TV shows. Clark will appear in a "reality-based" show about women in law enforcement, while Cochran is co-hosting a weekly commentary show on cable's Court TV.
